_README.purpose: Long-form comparison articles, served at /guides and /guides/<slug>. ONE source of truth. Read by src/lib/guides.ts (which src/pages/Guides.tsx and src/pages/GuideArticle.tsx use), by scripts/guides.mjs (which scripts/prerender.mjs uses for the crawlable body and scripts/static-routes.mjs uses for the routes and the sitemap), and by src/pages/CountryHub.tsx for the hub-to-article links. Nothing here is duplicated into a component, for the reason recorded in country-guides.json: a claim stated twice gets corrected once.
_README.whyItExists: Two AdSense rejections for low-value content, and Search Console showing impressions at an average position around 59. Volume was not the constraint; authority was. Nobody links to a directory entry, but people do cite a good comparison — so this section hosts the content type that can earn links.
_README.rules: CLAUDE.md content rules apply in full. Every factual claim traces to a government fisheries agency or a statutory licensing body. Articles cite countries by ISO code and the official links are resolved from country-guides.json at render time, so an article can never contradict the hub it sits beside. No bag limits, no size limits, no fees. No ratings and no review markup anywhere in this section: there are no reviews of an article, and fabricated ratings are a structured-data policy violation.
_README.shape: articles[] is ordered — the /guides index lists them in this order, newest first by convention. Per article: slug, title (the <title>, carries the site name), headline (the h1), description (meta, keep under about 155 characters), summary (the index-page teaser), datePublished and dateModified (ISO dates, used in Article JSON-LD), countries (ISO codes the article covers; this is what makes each country hub link to it), intro (blocks before the first heading) and sections[].
_README.sections: Each section is { heading, countries?, blocks }. `countries` is optional and renders that section's official sources — resolved live from country-guides.json — plus a link to each country hub. That is the promise the intro makes, and the internal linking is half the point of the section.
_README.blocks: Three block types, and adding a fourth means editing two renderers (scripts/prerender.mjs and src/pages/GuideArticle.tsx), so prefer composing what exists. { type: 'p', text } is a paragraph. { type: 'list', items } is a bulleted list. { type: 'table', columns, rows } is a comparison table. Inline markup inside any text is deliberately minimal — bold with double asterisks and italic with single — and is tokenised by the single shared parser in scripts/guide-inline.mjs so the prerendered HTML and the hydrated React cannot disagree about it. There is no markdown parser in the prerenderer and this file exists so that stays true.
_README.addingAnArticle: Data only. Append to articles[] and the route, the sitemap entry, the prerendered body, the Article JSON-LD, the /guides index card and the hub cross-links all follow. If you find yourself writing code to add an article, something above has been bypassed.

articles.title: Where to Fish If You Have Never Fished — AnglerDeck
articles.headline: Where to fish if you have never fished
articles.description: Seven genuinely beginner-friendly fishing destinations, and a few extraordinary ones worth saving for later. Drawn from AnglerDeck's own published spot guides.
articles.summary: Most of what gets written about these destinations assumes you already fish. This is the opposite list — real places, drawn straight from AnglerDeck's own spot pages, that are genuinely built for a first trip, plus a short list of what to save for later.

intro.text: Most fishing writing assumes a starting level most people don't have. This is the other list: places our own spot guides describe, in their own words, as genuinely approachable — no private beat, no lottery, no exam, nothing that assumes you've done this before.
Every entry here is a spot AnglerDeck already publishes and explicitly describes as accessible. It isn't every easy fishery in the world — it's the ones we've actually written up.

sections.heading: Freshwater lake systems built for a first trip

blocks.text: Three countries publish a lake system explicitly framed as an easy entry point, and they share a shape: large, connected, forgiving water rather than a technical river. Finland's Lake Saimaa is described in its own guide as one of the better beginner introductions to fishing anywhere — a maze of islands and channels fishable from a boat in summer and, unusually for a first-timer's destination, from the ice come February and March. Poland's Masurian Lake District is the same idea in Central Europe: a beginner-friendly maze of connected lakes holding pike, zander and perch. Germany's Müritz lakes round out the group, and carry a second advantage beyond ease of fishing — it's the one part of Germany a visitor can actually fish without sitting a state exam.

sections.heading: Accessible saltwater and an easy version of a famous river

blocks.text: Sweden's Stockholm archipelago is the standout for saltwater: beginner-friendly brackish water among thousands of islands, free to fish with a rod under Sweden's coastal access rule, and reachable in minutes from the capital — a rare combination of easy fishing and zero paperwork. Louisiana's Venice marsh is described the same way among its own country's spots, the beginner-friendly one of the four American entries, fishing redfish and speckled trout in shallow, forgiving marsh water. Canada's Bow River, meanwhile, isn't labelled beginner outright, but it's the most physically accessible of the country's three published rivers — a genuine trout tailwater running straight through the middle of Calgary, which counts for something when the alternative is a lodge with no road in.

sections.heading: A famous fish, made approachable

blocks.text: Two spots let you catch a genuinely famous fish without the hardest version of the fishery attached to it. New Zealand's Lake Taupō is explicitly the beginner-friendly counterpart to the Tongariro River next door — the same wild rainbow and brown trout, in a lake rather than technical running water, fished from boat or shore. Japan's Lake Yunoko at Nikkō is described the same way: beginner-friendly fly water for brook, rainbow and brown trout inside a national park. It's strictly catch-and-release, which is a real rule to know before you go, but it doesn't change how approachable the fishing itself is.

sections.heading: What to save for later

blocks.text: The flip side is worth naming too, because a first trip built around one of these will mostly teach frustration rather than fishing. Norway's Alta allocates access by lottery, largely to locals — advanced anglers plan years ahead, and that's before the fishing itself starts. All three of the UK's published spots are described as advanced fly water, with access running through private beats rather than anything a first-timer can simply book. Russia's two published fisheries are both advanced fly water reached by licensed camp, and Mexico's Ascension Bay is advanced flats fishing for bonefish, permit and tarpon — technical, sight-fished, and unforgiving of a first cast. None of these are bad choices. They're just not first choices.

sections.heading: Three things that trip up a first trip, none of them the fishing

blocks.text: Beginner-friendly water doesn't mean beginner-friendly paperwork, and the two aren't the same question. Germany's Müritz lakes are easy to fish and are also the one part of Germany you can fish without an exam — but elsewhere in the country, the exam applies regardless of how forgiving the water is. Worth reading the licensing comparison above before assuming "easy fishery" means "easy to arrange".

Approachable doesn't always mean rule-free, either. Lake Yunoko is genuinely beginner-friendly water and is also strictly catch-and-release — nothing may be removed from the lake. That's a real constraint to plan a first trip around, not a technicality.

And the closest good water to a major city is often better than it sounds. The Stockholm archipelago is minutes from a capital; the Bow River runs through the middle of Calgary; the Müritz lakes are a short drive from Berlin. A first trip doesn't have to mean a long one.

articles.title: A Year of Fishing Seasons, by Country — AnglerDeck
articles.headline: A year of fishing seasons, by country
articles.description: A month-by-month guide to when 19 countries actually fish best — from Norway's midnight-sun salmon to Argentina's Patagonian summer. Official and researched sources only.
articles.summary: Nineteen countries don't share one calendar — half run on the northern hemisphere's clock, some on the tropics' wet and dry seasons, a few on their own statutory closures entirely. This lays the year out month by month, so a trip gets planned around when a country actually fishes well, not just when it's convenient to fly.

intro.text: "Best time to fish" only makes sense per country, because the calendar underneath it changes completely depending where you're standing. Northern-hemisphere salmon rivers run to the midnight sun. Southern-hemisphere countries flip everything six months out of phase. The tropics run on wet and dry rather than summer and winter at all.
This groups the year into windows and places each of the 19 countries we cover into the one (or several) that fits, drawn from the same researched seasonal detail already on each country hub.

sections.heading: December–March: the southern hemisphere's best months

blocks.text: While the north is shut down for winter, the south is at its best. New Zealand's Bay of Islands runs its game-fishing season from January to May over the southern summer. South Africa's False Bay has yellowtail running November to April. Argentina's Río Grande sea trout peak January to March, fished in the evening as the wind eases. Mexico's Cabo San Lucas fishes striped marlin from October clean through to June, so it straddles this window rather than sitting inside it. Northern Australia is transitioning here too — the barramundi build-up runs October to December, ahead of the true wet-season run-off from February to April.

sections.heading: April–June: two hemispheres in transition

blocks.text: Europe's spring salmon runs open here — the Spey from April to May, Sweden's Mörrum from April to June — while France's Loire pike season opens once its closed season ends in spring. New Zealand's trout fishing flips the other way, its Tongariro rainbow run climbing from May onward. South Africa's Sodwana couta season starts in April. And in Brazil, this window sits inside the piracema spawning closure in most states, so it's the one country here where these months mean fishing is restricted rather than opening up — the Pantanal's dry season, and the fishing that comes with it, doesn't properly start until June.

sections.heading: June–August: peak northern summer, and the midnight sun

blocks.text: This is the far-northern window, and it's short and intense rather than a long summer season. Norway's Alta salmon peaks in June and July, fished through the night under a sun that never sets. Finland's Tornio runs the same window, June to August. Russia's Kola Peninsula salmon peak in June and July too, and Kamchatka's rainbow trout season runs July to September. In North America, Canada's Miramichi has its first salmon wave in June and July, and Alaska's Kenai River runs its heaviest sockeye push through July and August. Japan's Lake Yunoko fishes this stretch as its core season, April through September, with these months at the middle of it.

sections.heading: September–November: the second big flip

blocks.text: The calendar turns again here. Scotland's Tweed has its famous autumn run, September to November. Australia's Cairns marlin season is a defined heavy-tackle window from September to December. Louisiana's redfish run September to November. Canada's Miramichi has its second salmon wave here too, September and October, alongside Sweden's Stockholm archipelago pike (September to November) and its Mörrum autumn sea trout (September and October). Germany's Müritz lakes and Poland's Masurian lakes both fish pike best in this window. Argentina's Paraná dorado run September through April, so this is where that season opens.

sections.heading: The ones that run on their own clock

blocks.text: A handful of fisheries don't fit the four windows above at all. Norway's Lofoten skrei — migrating Arctic cod — arrive from January to April, making Lofoten a genuine winter destination while the rest of the country is closed down. Finland's Lake Saimaa becomes an ice fishery in February and March. Brazil's two fisheries run on dry-season water levels rather than temperature: the Pantanal from June to October, the Rio Negro from September to March. New Zealand's snapper and South Africa's False Bay tuna are both described as available essentially year-round, weather permitting, rather than keyed to a single run.

sections.heading: Season isn't the only thing to plan around

blocks.text: A country's best window only answers half the question. On rivers with lottery or booked-beat access — the Alta, Mörrum, and the private beats on the Spey and Tweed — the booking has to happen long before the season does, sometimes years ahead, independent of when the run actually peaks. Turning up at the right time of year on one of those rivers with no beat booked gets you nowhere. Elsewhere — New Zealand's snapper, South Africa's False Bay tuna, most saltwater flats fishing — access isn't the constraint and the season window above is genuinely the only thing to plan around.

The other thing worth factoring in: several of the closures and quotas mentioned above are reset annually rather than fixed on a calendar — Sweden's Mörrum, Finland and Norway's biosecurity rules, Brazil's piracema dates, Argentina's provincial seasons. A window that was open last year isn't a guarantee for this one.

articles.title: The World's Great Salmon Rivers, Compared — AnglerDeck
articles.headline: The world's great salmon rivers, compared
articles.description: Alta, Spey, Tweed, Mörrum, Tornio and Miramichi compared: how access, season and licensing actually differ on six storied Atlantic salmon rivers. Official sources only.
articles.summary: Six Atlantic salmon rivers, on four different licensing systems, with four different ways of deciding who gets to fish them — from a lottery in Arctic Norway to a river no country fully owns. What actually separates a great salmon river from another one isn't the fish. It's how you get access.

intro.text: Every storied salmon river gets described the same way — big, wild, legendary. What actually separates them has nothing to do with the fish and everything to do with how you get on the water: a lottery, a booked beat, a day ticket, or a run of luck with a river that two countries jointly manage.
This compares six rivers across five countries by access model and season rather than by reputation. Every claim traces to the national or regional agency responsible for the water.

sections.heading: Norway: one national rule, three very different rivers

blocks.text: The Alta, the Gaula and the Namsen all sit under the same Norwegian system: a national fishing fee for the season, plus a separate licence from whoever owns the riverbank, because the fee itself buys nothing beyond conservation funding. Where they differ sharply is what that second permit actually gets you.

The Alta, in Finnmark, is the hard one to get on: beats are allocated by lottery and largely reserved for locals, so access is very limited and advanced anglers plan years ahead. It peaks in June and July, fished through the night under the midnight sun. The Gaula and the Namsen, both in Trøndelag, are the more reachable Norwegian rivers by comparison — the Gaula known for long fly-friendly runs and a strong early-season run of large fish, the Namsen for big water traditionally fished by harling from a boat. Whatever river you choose, gear brought into Norway must be disinfected before it touches a salmon river — a biosecurity rule, not a formality.

sections.heading: Scotland: no rod licence anywhere, and the beat is everything

blocks.text: Scotland issues no salmon rod licence at all — a genuine outlier among the rivers here — which sounds like the simplest system on this list and is actually one of the hardest to arrange access on. Instead of a licence, you need a permit from whoever owns the beat: an estate, or a District Salmon Fishery Board. Nearly every beat on the Spey and the Tweed is private, so a day ticket, a syndicate rod or an estate booking is what actually gets you fishing, not a purchase from a national agency.

The two rivers run on opposite calendars. The Spey fishes a spring run in April and May and a summer grilse run from June to August. The Tweed is the autumn river — a September-to-November run that's among the best-known in Europe — with a smaller spring run from February to April, and it's administered separately from the England and Wales rod licence system entirely. Two Scottish rules apply to both: no salmon fishing on Sundays, and mandatory catch-and-release early in the season.

sections.heading: Sweden's Mörrum: booked beats and a season reset every year

blocks.text: Mörrum sits apart from the rest of Sweden's largely free-access fishing — a tightly managed Atlantic salmon and sea trout river fished on booked, numbered beats, the one Swedish river on this list where the permit is the whole game. Its spring run runs April to June and autumn sea trout come through in September and October, best when rain lifts the water. Unusually among these six rivers, its season dates, quotas and release rules are reset annually rather than fixed — last year's plan is explicitly not a guide to this year's rules.

sections.heading: Finland's Tornio: a river no single country fully governs

blocks.text: The Tornio forms the border between Finland and Sweden, and its management reflects that: season dates and quotas are agreed jointly between the two countries and change from year to year, rather than being set unilaterally by either. The run climbs from June to August, fished through bright midnight-sun nights and best after a rise in water. Like Norway, Finland requires gear disinfection on its salmon river — here specifically against *Gyrodactylus salaris*, a parasite that has devastated salmon stocks elsewhere in the region. Two countries with almost nothing else in common about how they license fishing agree on that one point.

sections.heading: Canada's Miramichi: two runs, and mostly a release fishery

blocks.text: The Miramichi in New Brunswick runs on Canada's provincial licensing system — a freshwater licence issued by the province, separate from the federal tidal-water system that governs British Columbia's saltwater fisheries. On the river itself, salmon arrive in two distinct waves: a summer run in June and July and an autumn run in September and October, both responding to rain lifting the water. It's largely a live-release fishery today, a conservation posture that sets it apart from rivers on this list where retention is the norm within a quota.

sections.heading: What actually separates these rivers

blocks.text: Strip away the scenery and four different access models are doing the real work of deciding who fishes:

items: **Lottery allocation** — the Alta. Demand so far exceeds capacity that access is randomised and mostly reserved for locals.
**Booked, numbered beats** — Mörrum, and most of the Spey and Tweed. A finite number of rods per day, sold or allotted per beat, with the estate or river authority controlling the calendar.
**Bilateral or shared management** — the Tornio, governed jointly by two national fisheries authorities rather than one.

**Provincial licence plus largely open access** — the Miramichi, where the barrier is the licence rather than a booking system, and much of today's fishery is catch-and-release by convention rather than by universal rule.

blocks.text: The pattern worth taking from this: on every river here, the licence or fee is rarely the hard part. Booking the water is. That's true even in Scotland, which charges no licence fee at all.

articles.title: Fishing Licences in Europe, Compared — AnglerDeck
articles.headline: Fishing licences in Europe, compared
articles.description: How fishing licences actually work across nine European countries, from Sweden's free coast to Germany's exam-only system. Official sources, no fees quoted.
articles.summary: Nine European countries, and nine different answers to "what do I actually need to fish here". Some issue a licence nationally, some regionally, some through a local association, and one makes you sit an exam. Every claim traces to the agency that made the rule.

intro.text: "Fishing licence" sounds like one thing. Across Europe it is at least four: a document you buy nationally, a document your region issues, membership of a local association, or — in one country — a document you can only get by passing an exam. None of these is more "correct" than another, but they change what a trip actually involves, and mixing them up is the easiest way to arrive somewhere with the wrong piece of paper.

This compares nine countries by how the system is built rather than by what it costs — fees change constantly and are left out everywhere on this site. Every claim below links to the agency, ministry or federation that made the rule.

sections.heading: Sweden and Norway: free water is the rule, not the exception

blocks.text: Sweden and Norway both start from a position most of the continent doesn't share: large amounts of water need no licence and no permission at all. In Sweden that's the entire coast plus five named lakes — Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren, Hjälmaren and Storsjön — where recreational rod fishing is simply free, under rules published jointly by the county boards and the national water management agency. Everywhere else in Sweden, fishing rights are private, and a *fiskekort* from the local fishing conservation area is what buys permission.

Norway draws a similar line in a different place: the sea is free nationwide, but rivers holding salmon, sea trout or Arctic char are not. There you pay a national fishing fee and, separately, a licence from whoever owns the riverbank — because in Norway the fee funds conservation, it does not buy access. **Neither country's free water is unregulated water.** Size rules and closed seasons still apply on both.

sections.heading: Germany: the one country where you sit an exam

blocks.text: Germany is the hardest country on this list to fish on impulse, and it's a genuine outlier in Europe for the reason why. Fishing law is set by each federal state, and the standard route to a *Fischereischein* is passing a state examination covering fish species, tackle, law and animal welfare — not something arranged in a weekend, let alone from abroad.

One state built a deliberate exception. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern issues a *Touristenfischereischein* with no exam at all, valid in its own coastal and inland waters for up to 28 consecutive days and renewable within the same calendar year. It's the one place in Germany a visitor can realistically turn up and fish. Everywhere else, the licence is only step one — a further *Erlaubnisschein* is needed for the specific water regardless of which route got you the Fischereischein.

sections.heading: France and Poland: two separate documents, not one

blocks.text: France and Poland both split freshwater fishing into two layers, and both catch visitors who only arrange one of them. In France, the *carte de pêche* is really membership of a local AAPPMA — an approved fishing and aquatic-environment association — sold nationally through the federation's own site as daily, weekly or annual cards. That covers fresh water. Sea angling sits outside the carte de pêche system entirely, under the maritime fishing code instead, and since a ministerial order in force from early 2026, recreational sea anglers aged 16 and over targeting listed species must separately register and declare those catches the day they're taken.

Poland's split runs the other way: one document authorises the angler, a second authorises the water. The *karta wędkarska* — the fishing card, issued by the district authority — is what lets you fish at all. A separate *zezwolenie*, a permit for the specific fishing ground, comes from whoever holds the rights there; for the many waters managed by the state water authority, Wody Polskie, that permit has been sold exclusively online since January 2026, as a QR-coded PDF rather than a physical card.

sections.heading: Spain and Italy: sea fishing that reports itself

blocks.text: Spain and Italy both license sea fishing in a way that's less about buying a permit up front and more about ongoing digital reporting. Spain issues recreational licences regionally — one autonomous community's licence doesn't cover another — and layers a national system, PescaREC, on top: anglers register and report their catches daily through the app, whether fishing from shore, a boat or underwater.

Italian sea fishing is free of charge but not free of process. The national ministry, MASAF, operates a sport-fishing census that recreational sea anglers must file a notification through — and the practical difficulty for visitors is the login, which has run exclusively through Italian digital identity credentials (SPID, the electronic ID card, or the national services card) since 2022. That's worth resolving with a charter operator before a trip, not at the harbour. Freshwater in Italy runs on an entirely separate, regional system instead.

sections.heading: United Kingdom and Finland: licence-free doesn't mean permission-free

blocks.text: Scotland issues no rod licence at all for salmon fishing — and is simultaneously one of the hardest places on this list to actually get on the water, because access runs entirely through private riparian rights, let out beat by beat via estates and angling associations. England and Wales are the opposite: an Environment Agency rod licence is required, explicitly including on private club lakes, but the licence is permission to hold a rod, not permission to fish a given water — the owner's consent is still a separate matter.

Finland threads a middle path. Its state fisheries management fee, payable by anglers aged 18 to 69 fishing with lures, is by itself sufficient permission for single-rod fishing across much of the country — genuinely rare in Europe. But fishing with several rods, in rapids or flowing water, or at most of the country's better-known sites additionally needs a permit from the water owner, so the good rivers generally need both layers anyway.

sections.heading: What actually differs, underneath the details

blocks.text: Strip away the specifics and three questions separate every system on this list, and they're worth asking before any trip:

items: **Who issues it?** National (France, Italy, Spain's PescaREC layer), regional or state (Germany, Spain's base licence, Italy's freshwater licence), or local association (France's AAPPMA, Poland's water-specific permit).
**Does it require an exam?** Only Germany, and only outside Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's tourist exception.

**Does holding it mean you can actually fish a given water, or is that a separate question?** In England and Wales, Poland, and both Norwegian and French freshwater, the licence and the water-access permission are explicitly two different things. In Sweden's free waters and Scotland, the licence question doesn't arise at all — but Scotland still gates access through the beat owner.

blocks.text: The pattern worth remembering: a country that looks licence-free on paper (Scotland, Norway's sea, Sweden's coast) has usually moved the real gatekeeping somewhere else — to the landowner, the beat, or the association — rather than removed it.

articles.title: Where You Can Fish Without a Licence — AnglerDeck
articles.headline: Where you can fish without a licence
articles.description: Which countries let you fish without a licence, and which only look like they do. Norway, Sweden, New Zealand, the UK and more, with official sources.
articles.summary: A country-by-country comparison of where recreational fishing needs no licence — and where "no licence" still does not mean "no permission". Every claim links to the agency that made the rule.

intro.text: Most fishing advice starts with "buy a licence". It is good advice almost everywhere — but not everywhere, and the exceptions are more useful than they look. If you are planning a trip, knowing which waters you can simply walk up to and fish changes what is worth flying for.

This is a comparison drawn from the nineteen countries we cover; eleven of them have something worth saying on this question. Every claim links to the agency that made the rule. Two warnings before the list: free never means unregulated, and "no licence" rarely means "no permission needed". Both catch people out, and we come back to them at the end.

sections.heading: Norway: the sea is free, the rivers are not

blocks.text: Norway draws the cleanest line of any country here. The Norwegian Environment Agency confirms you do not need to pay the national fishing fee to fish with a rod or hand line in the sea — and you may fish there for salmon, sea trout and Arctic char from the shore year-round, subject to local bylaws.
That is an unusually generous position. Sea-run salmon from the shore, no paperwork.

Fresh water is the opposite. For rivers and lakes holding anadromous fish you must pay the national fishing fee before fishing during the ordinary season, carry proof, and produce it on request. And the fee is not permission to fish — fishing rights belong to the landowner, so you need their licence as well. On a river like the Alta, that landowner permit is the real bottleneck, not the fee.

sections.heading: Sweden: free coast, and five free lakes

blocks.text: Sweden has the most generous access rules on this list, and the boundary is geographic rather than bureaucratic. Along the entire coast, and on the five great lakes — Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren, Hjälmaren and Storsjön in Jämtland — recreational rod fishing is free.
That is not a technicality. Vänern is the largest lake in the European Union. You can fish it, with a rod, without buying anything.

Outside those waters, fishing rights are private. Most managed waters are organised into fishing conservation areas selling a *fiskekort*, and the Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management maps them — species, permit sellers and all — so a specific water is easy to check before you travel.

sections.heading: New Zealand: free at sea, one trap inland

blocks.text: Sea fishing in New Zealand needs no licence at all. The freshwater rules are the only paperwork most visitors face, and they contain a trap worth knowing: a Fish & Game licence covers the whole country **except** the Taupō district, which the Department of Conservation administers separately. A Fish & Game licence is not valid there. Lake Rotoaira is a third district again, with its own licences.
Since Taupō is one of the best trout fisheries on earth, this catches a lot of people.

sections.heading: United Kingdom: sea angling free, fresh water split in two

blocks.text: Sea angling is free throughout the UK. Fresh water is really two systems.

In England and Wales you need an Environment Agency rod licence to fish for salmon, trout, freshwater fish, smelt or eel with a rod and line — and GOV.UK is explicit that this applies on private water too, club lakes included. The licence permits you to hold a rod; it is not permission to fish a particular water, so you still need the owner's consent.

Scotland issues no rod licence at all. Instead you need a permit from whoever owns the beat, usually an estate or a District Salmon Fishery Board. So Scotland is simultaneously licence-free and among the harder places to arrange access.
Children under 13 need no licence in England and Wales; 13-to-16-year-olds hold a free junior one.

sections.heading: Australia: it depends entirely which state you are standing in

blocks.text: There is no Australian fishing licence. Each state and territory runs its own system, and the gap between neighbours is wide.

The **Northern Territory requires no recreational licence whatsoever** — though boating rules, closed areas and Aboriginal land permissions all still apply. **New South Wales** sits at the other end: the Recreational Fishing Fee covers both fresh and salt water, and you must carry proof while fishing. NSW does publish exemptions, including anglers fishing under a guide or charter operator holding an exemption certificate.
On border rivers like the Murray, which bank you are standing on decides whose rules apply.

sections.heading: Japan and Russia: no licence, but not open access

blocks.text: Japan has no recreational fishing licence in the European sense. The Fisheries Agency treats recreational fishing as "minor capture" and sets out what foreign nationals may do by method and vessel: from shore, rod, hand line, net and spear fishing are permitted. Inland waters are different — local fisheries cooperatives set rules approved by the prefectural governor, including a fee and a permit called a *yugyoken*.

Russia likewise has no recreational licence, and the Federal Agency for Fishery states that public waters may be fished freely and free of charge, subject to the fishing rules for the relevant basin. But on designated fishing grounds — which is what the famous salmon and trout rivers are — fishing runs under a *putyovka*, a paid-services contract specifying catch, area, methods and period. Those fisheries are booked commercially, well in advance.

sections.heading: Free of charge, but not free of paperwork

blocks.text: Three countries charge nothing for sea angling, or nothing beyond a regional licence, and still require you to file something.

**Italy**: sea fishing is free of charge, but MASAF operates a sport-fishing census through which recreational sea anglers must file a *comunicazione*. The practical catch is the login — access has run exclusively through Italian digital identity credentials (SPID, electronic ID card, or national services card) since 2022, which most visitors do not hold. Resolve it with a charter operator before travelling, not at the harbour.

**Spain**: on top of a regional licence, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food runs PescaREC, an app through which sea anglers register and report catches daily — from shore as well as from a boat.

**France**: fresh water needs a *carte de pêche*, which is really membership of a local AAPPMA association. The sea sits outside that system — but since 2026 it is not outside the paperwork. The maritime fishing code subjects recreational sea fishing to the same provisions as professional fishing on minimum sizes, permitted gear, zones and periods, and allows specific recreational activities to be made subject to authorisation by ministerial order. One such order now applies broadly: sea anglers aged 16 and over targeting the species it lists must register — a registration valid twelve months, through the European Commission's recreational fisheries platform or the RecFishing app — and must declare catches of those species on the day they are taken.

We looked hard for an official page stating that French sea angling needs no licence, because it would have been the most useful line in this article. There is not one. Légifrance shows only that authorisation regimes *may* be imposed on activities listed by order, which is not the same as a statement that none applies to ordinary rod-and-line fishing, and the ministry's own page discusses the new registration duty and nothing else. So France appears here for its paperwork, and not in the licence-free column.

sections.heading: Age exemptions worth knowing

blocks.text: **Finland** applies its state fisheries management fee to anglers aged 18 to 69 fishing with lures. Outside that band, no fee. Finland's everyman's-right tradition also leaves simple methods — ice fishing, basic float fishing — outside the fee regime entirely, which is why a Finnish winter trip involves almost no paperwork.
**England and Wales**: under-13s free, 13–16 free junior licence.

sections.heading: The two things that catch people out

blocks.text: **Free does not mean unregulated.** Sweden's free waters still carry size rules and closed seasons. Norway's free sea fishing is still subject to local bylaws. The Northern Territory still has closed areas. Removing the licence removes one requirement, not the rest.

**No licence is not the same as permission.** This is the one that costs people a day's fishing. In Norway, paying the national fee does not entitle you to fish — the landowner still has to sell you a permit. In Scotland there is no licence at all, but you cannot fish without the beat owner's say-so. In England and Wales the rod licence is explicitly not permission to fish a given water. In Finland, the state fee covers single-rod fishing in much of the country, but the good rivers and rapids need the water owner's permit too.
The pattern: countries that removed the licence usually did so because fishing rights sit with landowners instead. The paperwork moved rather than disappeared.
